content_voiceover: This table is a high-yield way to use hepcidin as a diagnostic tool across anemia types. In simple iron deficiency anemia, hepcidin is appropriately low, transferrin saturation and ferritin are low, and soluble transferrin receptor is increased, reflecting marrow demand for iron. IRIDA breaks that pattern: hepcidin is paradoxically high despite low TSAT and low ferritin, because TMPRSS6 can't shut hepcidin off. Anemia with iron overload shows low hepcidin in the non-transfused state with high TSAT and ferritin, the opposite problem. Anemia of chronic disease, driven by inflammatory cytokines like IL-6, has high hepcidin, low TSAT, but ferritin normal or high, and critically, soluble transferrin receptor stays normal, since marrow iron stores aren't actually depleted, just sequestered. That sTfR distinction is the classic way boards ask you to separate ACD from true IDA when ferritin is equivocal. Mixed anemia, meaning IDA plus ACD together, gives you normal hepcidin with variable ferritin and sTfR, a genuinely difficult diagnostic gray zone. Finally, anemia of chronic kidney disease and EPO resistance both show high hepcidin with variable everything else, reflecting hepcidin-driven functional iron restriction as a mechanism of EPO hyporesponsiveness in dialysis patients.
keypoints: IDA: hepcidin low, TSAT/ferritin low, sTfR increased
ACD: hepcidin high, ferritin normal/high, sTfR normal — key differentiator from IDA
IRIDA: hepcidin high despite iron deficiency (TMPRSS6)
Iron overload (non-transfused): hepcidin low, TSAT/ferritin high
ACKD & EPO resistance: hepcidin high, functional iron restriction
keypoint_voiceover: Use hepcidin plus soluble transferrin receptor to split the difficult cases. True iron deficiency has low hepcidin and a high soluble transferrin receptor. Anemia of chronic disease has high hepcidin but a normal soluble transferrin receptor, since stores aren't actually depleted. IRIDA looks like iron deficiency but hepcidin is paradoxically high. Iron overload shows the reverse, low hepcidin with high saturation and ferritin. And in chronic kidney disease or EPO resistance, hepcidin is elevated and drives functional iron restriction.
